nodeData.note: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, PSB, KMB, mycorrhiza — and how to use bio-inputs well.

children.note: Rhizobia are bacteria that form pink nodules on legume roots and fix air nitrogen for the plant. Using the right strain for each crop group, applied carefully on seed, can supply much of a legume's nitrogen.

Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen and releases growth hormones near roots of non-legume crops. It works best in soils rich in organic matter and complements, not replaces, good fertility.

Nitrogen-fixing helpers for non-legume crops: Azospirillum on cereal roots, Gluconacetobacter inside sugarcane, and cyanobacteria and Azolla in rice fields. They supply part of the crop's nitrogen and improve rooting.

Soil bacteria and fungi that release phosphorus locked up as calcium, iron or aluminium phosphates. Used with compost and rock phosphate, they help crops get more from the phosphorus already in the soil.
Soil bacteria that unlock potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron already present in soil or minerals. They complement fertilisers and work best with organic matter and moisture.

Soil fungi that partner with plant roots, extending them with fine hyphae to bring in phosphorus, zinc and water in exchange for plant sugars. Most crops benefit; protecting native fungi matters as much as adding inoculum.
Biofertilizers and biopesticides are living products. They only work if they arrive alive, are applied the right way, and are used as part of a wider soil and crop plan.

nodeData.note: Rhizobia are bacteria that form pink nodules on legume roots and fix air nitrogen for the plant. Using the right strain for each crop group, applied carefully on seed, can supply much of a legume's nitrogen.

children.note: Rhizobia are soil bacteria that live in partnership with legume plants and turn air nitrogen into a form the plant can use.
Rhizobia are rod-shaped, Gram-negative soil bacteria. On their own in soil they do little for nitrogen; their value comes when they enter a legume root.

manas.q: What type of organism is Rhizobium, and which plants does it partner with?

children.note: The group called rhizobia includes Rhizobium, Bradyrhizobium, Mesorhizobium and Sinorhizobium (also called Ensifer), among others. Each genus tends to suit different legume crops.

manas.q: Name four genera of rhizobia.

children.note: Unlike Azotobacter, rhizobia fix meaningful nitrogen only inside root nodules, where the plant supplies sugar and a low-oxygen home.

manas.q: Does Rhizobium fix useful nitrogen while free in the soil?

children.note: A given rhizobial strain nodulates only a certain set of legumes. That is why inoculants are sold per crop group, not as one product for every legume.
The legume and the bacterium exchange chemical signals, build a nodule together, and then trade sugar for fixed nitrogen.
Legume roots release flavonoids. Matching rhizobia answer with Nod factors, signal molecules that tell the root to start forming a nodule.

manas.q: What signal molecules do rhizobia send to the legume root?

children.topic: Root hair curl and infection thread
children.note: The root hair curls around the bacteria and a tube called the infection thread carries them inward to dividing root cells.
Inside the new nodule the bacteria change into bacteroids, the form that actually fixes nitrogen.
The enzyme nitrogenase converts air nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant builds into proteins. The process costs the plant a lot of energy.

manas.q: Which enzyme converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia in the nodule?

children.note: Nitrogenase is damaged by oxygen. The plant makes leghaemoglobin, a red pigment that binds oxygen and gives active nodules their pink colour.

manas.q: Why are active nodules pink inside?

children.note: In return for nitrogen the plant feeds the bacteroids with carbon from photosynthesis, so a healthy, well-lit crop supports better fixation.
Roots, nodules and residues of a well-nodulated legume leave some nitrogen in the soil, which helps a following cereal crop.
A cross-inoculation group is a set of legumes that can be nodulated by the same rhizobia. Use the inoculant made for your crop's group.
Legumes in one group share compatible rhizobia; an inoculant from another group usually forms few or no working nodules.

manas.q: What is a cross-inoculation group?

children.note: Soybean needs its own slow-growing Bradyrhizobium strains. Where soybean is new to a field, native soil rarely has them, so inoculation is especially important.

manas.q: Which rhizobium is used for soybean?

children.note: Chickpea (Bengal gram) is nodulated by Mesorhizobium strains specific to chickpea; it forms its own group.

manas.q: Which rhizobium group nodulates chickpea?

children.note: These share Rhizobium leguminosarum (biovar viciae), so one pea-group inoculant suits them.
French and common beans use bean-group strains such as R. phaseoli, R. etli and R. tropici. In Kenya, bean is the most widely inoculated legume.
Cowpea, groundnut, pigeonpea, green gram and black gram fall in the broad cowpea group, mostly nodulated by Bradyrhizobium.

manas.q: Name three crops in the cowpea cross-inoculation group.

children.note: Lucerne (alfalfa), fenugreek (methi) and sweet clover are nodulated by Sinorhizobium meliloti.
Clovers (Trifolium, incl. berseem) form a group with R. leguminosarum biovar trifolii.
TNAU lists approximate fixation of about 57–105 kg N/ha for soybean and cowpea-group crops, 75–117 for chickpea and 62–132 for pea and lentil, depending on conditions.
Checking nodules is the simplest way to know if Rhizobium is working. Dig, don't pull, and cut nodules open.
Dig up a few plants with soil around the roots at early flowering, wash gently in water and look at the crown of the main root.
Slice a nodule with a blade. A pink to red centre shows leghaemoglobin and active nitrogen fixation.

manas.q: What colour is the inside of an effective nodule?

children.topic: White, green or grey = not fixing
children.note: White insides mean the nodule is young or ineffective; green or grey means it is old or failing, often after drought or waterlogging.

manas.q: What does a white or green nodule interior indicate?

children.note: Large nodules clustered on the upper taproot usually come from the inoculant on the seed; small scattered ones on side roots are often native, less effective strains.
Soybean, bean and groundnut form round nodules; pea, chickpea and alfalfa form longer, finger-like or branched nodules. Both shapes can be effective.
Wrong or dead inoculant, hot or dry treated seed, acid soil, high fertilizer nitrogen, seed fungicide mixed with inoculant, or waterlogging.

manas.q: List three common reasons for poor or no nodulation.

children.note: Inoculate whenever a legume is new to a field, or past crops showed poor nodules or pale plants.
If the crop (or its group) has not been grown recently, matching rhizobia are probably absent and inoculation gives the biggest benefit.

manas.q: When is inoculating a legume most likely to pay off?

children.note: Uniform yellowing starting from older, lower leaves in a legume often means nodules are not supplying enough nitrogen.
Many pink nodules, dark green leaves without added nitrogen and vigorous growth through flowering and pod filling.
Acid soils, drought, waterlogging and very high soil temperatures reduce nodule formation and fixation.
When much mineral nitrogen is available, the plant forms fewer nodules. A small starter dose is fine; heavy urea defeats the purpose.

manas.q: What happens to nodulation when large amounts of nitrogen fertilizer are applied?

children.note: Nodules need phosphorus for energy, molybdenum for nitrogenase and calcium for infection. Deficient soils give weak fixation even with good inoculant.

manas.q: Which micronutrient is part of the nitrogenase enzyme?

children.note: Rhizobium inoculants are living products. Form, count and freshness matter more than the price.
Bacteria grown in a fine carrier such as peat or lignite. Cheap and common; mixed with a sticker and coated on seed.
Bacteria in a broth with protectants. Liquids are easier to dose, need less volume per acre and usually keep longer than powders.
Granular inoculants are placed in the seed furrow; useful when seed carries fungicide or is too delicate to coat.
TNAU notes carrier packets should hold above 10⁹ cells/g when made and at least 10⁷ cells/g up to expiry. Always check the count and the crop group printed on the pack.
TNAU gives roughly 12–24 months for liquid formulations; carrier packets are shorter-lived. Never use past the expiry date.
Keep packs in a cool, dry, shaded place away from heat and direct sun; never leave them in a hot vehicle or shop window.

manas.q: How should Rhizobium inoculant be stored?

children.note: In India biofertilizers must meet Fertiliser Control Order (FCO) standards. In Kenya, inoculants are regulated through KEPHIS and related bodies; buy registered products only.
Seed coating is the standard way to apply Rhizobium. Work in the shade and sow the same day.
Boil a little jaggery (gur) or rice gruel in water and let it cool fully. Hot sticker kills the bacteria.

manas.q: What is jaggery or rice gruel used for in seed inoculation?

children.note: Stir the inoculant into the cool sticker to make an even slurry. TNAU's carrier method uses one 200 g packet in 200 ml rice gruel.
Spread seed on a clean sheet or in a bag and mix with the slurry by hand until every seed has a thin coat, without breaking seed coats.
Air-dry the coated seed in shade for about half an hour. Sunlight and heat quickly kill rhizobia.

manas.q: Why must inoculated seed be dried in shade, not sun?

children.note: Sow within a few hours, and not later than 24 hours, into moist soil and cover it promptly.
TNAU suggests about 200 ml liquid per acre of pulse seed, or one 200 g carrier packet per about 10 kg seed. Follow the product label.
If seed must be treated with fungicide, apply it first, let it dry, then inoculate just before sowing; never mix them in one slurry.

manas.q: If seed needs fungicide, in what order are fungicide and Rhizobium applied?

children.note: Rhizobium can be combined with phosphate-solubilising bacteria; TNAU advises Rhizobium on the seed first and PSB as the outer layer.
Living bacteria die from heat, sun, chemicals and time.
Do not mix inoculant with chemical fertilizers, insecticides, fungicides or herbicides.
Keep treated seed and packs out of the sun and sow into moist soil so bacteria survive until roots emerge.

children.topic: Use the whole pack at once
children.note: Once opened, a pack starts losing viable bacteria; use it the same day.
In acid soils, a fine coat of lime or rock phosphate over inoculated seed helps protect rhizobia.
Well-decomposed FYM or compost supports soil biology and does not harm the inoculant.
Good inoculation can supply much of a legume's own nitrogen needs and leave some for the next crop, but results vary with soil and season.
A well-nodulated legume usually needs little or no extra nitrogen beyond a small starter dose.
Responses are strongest in fields new to the crop; where native strains are plentiful, gains may be small.

children.topic: Not a substitute for P and K
children.note: Rhizobium supplies only nitrogen. Phosphorus, potassium, sulphur and micronutrients still need managing.
Cereals after a good legume crop often grow better thanks to residual nitrogen and improved soil.
Most failures come from handling, not from the bacteria.

children.topic: Myth: one inoculant for all legumes
children.note: Strains are group-specific. Soybean inoculant will not help chickpea, and the reverse.

children.topic: Mistake: checking too early or late
children.note: Very young plants have tiny nodules and old plants have spent ones. Check around early flowering.
Heavy nitrogen fertilizer makes the plant stop forming nodules, so it wastes both the inoculant and the urea.

children.topic: Myth: lots of nodules means success
children.note: Many small white nodules may fix nothing. Colour inside matters more than number.
The N2Africa project worked with Kenyan farmers on bean and soybean inoculation and promoted pairing inoculant with phosphorus fertilizer.

nodeData.note: Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen and releases growth hormones near roots of non-legume crops. It works best in soils rich in organic matter and complements, not replaces, good fertility.

children.note: Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen without forming nodules.
It fixes nitrogen while living freely in soil and around roots, and it needs oxygen to live.

manas.q: Is Azotobacter symbiotic or free-living, and does it need oxygen?

children.note: The most common species in farm soils and the one most used in biofertilizers. Its cultures turn brown to black with age.

manas.q: Which Azotobacter species is most common in arable soils and biofertilizers?

children.note: A closely related species widely studied in laboratories; it has backup nitrogenases that can work when molybdenum is scarce.

manas.q: Which Azotobacter species is known for alternative (vanadium) nitrogenases?

children.note: Cells are large, oval rods that often occur in pairs and produce plenty of slime.
It is common in the soil around roots (rhizosphere) but does not enter root tissue or form nodules.

manas.q: Does Azotobacter form root nodules?

children.note: As it cannot make its own food, it depends on organic matter and root exudates; poor, low-carbon soils hold few cells.
Azotobacter helps plants mainly through nitrogen fixation and plant growth substances.
Like rhizobia it uses nitrogenase to turn N₂ into ammonia, but it does so on its own using soil carbon for energy.
It breathes very fast, using up oxygen inside the cell so the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase can keep working.

manas.q: How does aerobic Azotobacter protect nitrogenase from oxygen?

children.note: Under stress it forms thick-walled cysts that resist drying; they germinate into active cells when moisture and food return.

manas.q: What resting structure does Azotobacter form to survive drought?

children.note: It releases growth substances such as indole acetic acid (an auxin), gibberellins and cytokinins that encourage root growth and germination.

manas.q: Name three plant growth hormones produced by Azotobacter.

children.note: B vitamins and other compounds it releases support seedling vigour and root branching.
Its polysaccharide slime (alginate) helps bind soil particles into aggregates.
TNAU notes Azotobacter produces substances that inhibit several soil fungi, a minor protective effect.
Azotobacter is meant for non-legume crops.
Wheat, maize, barley, oats, sorghum, pearl and finger millet respond to seed treatment.
Tomato, brinjal, chilli, cabbage, cauliflower, onion and others, by seedling root dip or soil application.
Cotton, mustard, sunflower, sesame and castor are listed crops for seed treatment.
Sugarcane setts, tea, coffee, coconut, fruit trees and nursery plants via soil or sett treatment.
Useful in nurseries and upland rice; in flooded paddy, Azospirillum and blue-green algae are generally preferred.
For pulses and soybeans, Rhizobium is the main nitrogen inoculant; Azotobacter is not a substitute.

manas.q: Should Azotobacter replace Rhizobium for legumes?

children.note: Azotobacter does best in well-aerated, near-neutral soils rich in organic matter.
Without enough organic carbon the bacteria cannot multiply; pair it with compost or FYM.

manas.q: What soil condition most limits Azotobacter numbers?

children.note: It performs poorly in strongly acidic soils; liming or Azospirillum may be better there.

manas.q: How does Azotobacter cope with acidic soils?

children.note: Moist but not waterlogged soil suits it; prolonged flooding limits this aerobic organism.
Low-input or organic fields, crops showing pale older leaves from nitrogen shortage, and soils low in biological activity.
There is no nodule to inspect; look for better germination, stronger roots and greener growth than untreated strips.

manas.q: How can a farmer judge if Azotobacter is working, since it forms no nodules?

children.note: Sold as carrier powder, liquid, granules, or in NPK consortia.
Bacteria in lignite or similar carrier; mixed with sticker for seed or with compost for soil.
Broth with protectants; easier dosing. TNAU gives roughly 12–24 months shelf life for liquids.
Ready for broadcasting or furrow application with manure.
Combined with phosphate-solubilising and potash-mobilising bacteria in one product for broad nutrient support.
Check the viable count, species, crop list and expiry on the pack; India's FCO sets minimum counts for sale.
Keep cool, dry and shaded, away from sun and chemicals; never use after expiry.

manas.q: How should Azotobacter products be stored?

children.note: India: FCO biofertilizer standards. Kenya: products should be registered with the relevant authorities (e.g. KEPHIS); avoid unlabelled products.
Choose seed, seedling or soil application by crop; work in shade and keep away from chemicals.
Mix inoculant with a cooled jaggery or rice gruel sticker, coat seed, dry in shade and sow the same day.
TNAU lists about 200 ml liquid per acre for seed treatment of wheat, millets, oilseeds and forage grasses.
For transplanted vegetables, dip roots in a suspension of inoculant in water for a short time before planting.
Mix with well-rotted FYM or compost, keep moist in shade for a few days, then spread before sowing or along rows.

manas.q: Why is Azotobacter mixed with compost or FYM for soil application?

children.note: Liquid can go through drip; TNAU lists about 2–3 ml per plant for coconut, fruit and nursery plants.
Apply at sowing or planting so bacteria establish with young roots; repeat soil application in long-duration crops if advised.
Do not mix with chemical fertilizers, fungicides or bactericides; separate by several days and apply fungicide first on seed.

manas.q: Can Azotobacter be mixed directly with chemical fungicides?

children.note: Azotobacter is a supplement that supports nitrogen supply and root growth, not a full replacement for fertilizer.
It can contribute some of the crop's nitrogen, so part of mineral N may be reduced; responses vary with soil carbon.
Trials commonly report modest yield improvements, mostly from hormone-driven root growth plus nitrogen.
TNAU notes Indian soils rarely hold more than about 10⁵ Azotobacter per gram, which is why inoculation can help.
Results are best where compost, mulches and residues feed soil life.
Common errors that waste the product.
It fixes far less than a legume–Rhizobium partnership; crops still need balanced nutrition.

manas.q: Does Azotobacter fully replace nitrogen fertilizer?

children.note: Without organic matter the bacteria starve; always add compost or manure.
Tank-mixing with fungicides or fertilizers kills the bacteria.
Heat and sun kill cells on treated seed; dry in shade and sow quickly.
Old or heat-exposed products may contain few living cells.

nodeData.note: Nitrogen-fixing helpers for non-legume crops: Azospirillum on cereal roots, Gluconacetobacter inside sugarcane, and cyanobacteria and Azolla in rice fields. They supply part of the crop's nitrogen and improve rooting.

children.topic: The big idea: N for non-legumes
children.note: Legumes get nitrogen from Rhizobium nodules, but cereals, millets and sugarcane have no nodules. A group of bacteria and cyanobacteria can still fix air nitrogen near, on or inside these crops.
Grasses such as maize, rice and sugarcane are heavy nitrogen feeders and depend almost entirely on soil and fertilizer N. Associative and free-living fixers add a modest extra supply.

manas.q: Why do cereals benefit from Azospirillum when they have no nodules?

children.topic: Three ways to live with a plant
children.note: Associative fixers (Azospirillum) live on and in roots; endophytes (Gluconacetobacter) live inside plant tissue; free-living cyanobacteria fix N in flood water. Azolla hosts Anabaena as a true symbiont.

manas.q: Name the lifestyle of Azospirillum, Gluconacetobacter and Anabaena in Azolla.

children.note: The enzyme that fixes nitrogen, nitrogenase, is damaged by oxygen. Each organism protects it differently: Azospirillum prefers low-oxygen zones and cyanobacteria fix N in thick-walled heterocysts.

manas.q: Which enzyme fixes nitrogen, and what damages it?

children.note: These organisms supply part of the crop's N and improve roots. They work alongside compost, manure and reduced fertilizer, not as a full substitute in most fields.
A soil bacterium that colonises the root surface and outer root tissue of grasses and cereals. It is one of the most widely used biofertilizers for non-legume crops in India.
Azospirillum brasilense and Azospirillum lipoferum are the species most used in inoculants. Both are Gram-negative, motile, curved rod-shaped bacteria.

manas.q: Which two Azospirillum species are most common in biofertilizers?

children.note: It does not form nodules. It lives in close association with roots, in the rhizosphere and in spaces of the root cortex, feeding on root exudates.

manas.q: Does Azospirillum form root nodules?

children.note: It fixes nitrogen best where oxygen is low but not absent, such as the root surface and moist soil. It swims toward roots using flagella.

manas.q: What does microaerophilic mean for Azospirillum?

children.note: It helps the crop in two ways: fixing some atmospheric nitrogen and, often more importantly, producing hormones that build a bigger root system.

children.topic: Fixes nitrogen in the root zone
children.note: It converts air nitrogen into ammonium that partly becomes available to the plant. TNAU cites about 20–40 kg N/ha for non-legume crops under good conditions.

manas.q: Roughly how much N can Azospirillum supply (TNAU)?

children.note: It releases indole-acetic acid, gibberellins and other growth substances. These cause more root hairs and lateral roots.

manas.q: Which plant hormone is Azospirillum best known for producing?

children.note: A larger root system takes up more water, phosphorus and micronutrients. This root effect explains much of its yield benefit.
Better-rooted plants cope better with short dry spells. TNAU also mentions improved drought tolerance and some disease resistance.

children.topic: Sign it is needed: yellow older leaves
children.note: Nitrogen shortage shows first as pale yellowing of older, lower leaves, often in a V-shape from the tip in maize. Growth is slow and thin.

manas.q: Where does N-deficiency yellowing appear first?

children.note: Expect stronger, hairier roots and steady green colour, not an overnight change. Compare treated and untreated strips in the same field.
Best suited to grasses and cereals, with reported use on a range of other non-legume crops.
These are the classic Azospirillum crops. Finger millet, pearl millet and sorghum respond well in low-input farming.

manas.q: Name four classic crops for Azospirillum.

children.note: Used for wheat and barley, often together with or instead of Azotobacter.
TNAU lists cotton and oilseeds; in South India it is also used on sugarcane together with phosphate solubilizers.
Relevant to maize, sorghum, millet and irrigated rice schemes. Use only registered products and test on a small area first.
An N-fixing bacterium that lives inside sugarcane. It was first described as Acetobacter diazotrophicus and later renamed Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus.
Older labels say Acetobacter diazotrophicus; the current name is Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus. Both refer to the same organism.

manas.q: What is the current name of Acetobacter diazotrophicus?

children.note: It lives inside the plant: in roots, stems and leaves of sugarcane. Being inside protects it from competition with soil microbes.

manas.q: Is Gluconacetobacter an endophyte or a soil free-living bacterium?

children.note: It thrives in sugary, acidic conditions like cane sap, which few other bacteria tolerate. That makes sugarcane its natural home.

manas.q: Why is sugarcane a good home for Gluconacetobacter?

children.note: Mainly sugarcane; also found in sweet sorghum and sweet potato.
Some Brazilian sugarcane varieties obtain part of their N from biological fixation, and Gluconacetobacter was found studying them. Benefits elsewhere depend on variety and conditions.
Usually by soaking setts in the bacterial suspension before planting, plus soil application with well-rotted FYM. Follow the label for dose and soaking time.
Some sources quote large yield and sugar gains; results in farmer fields vary. Treat it as one part of cane nutrition, not a stand-alone N source.
Photosynthetic bacteria that fix nitrogen in flooded rice fields. Using them as a biofertilizer is called algalization.
Despite the name, blue-green algae are cyanobacteria. They make their own food from sunlight and many also fix nitrogen.

manas.q: Are blue-green algae true algae?

children.note: Thick-walled special cells called heterocysts keep oxygen out so nitrogenase can work. Anabaena and Nostoc form chains with these cells.

manas.q: What is a heterocyst?

children.note: Nostoc, Anabaena, Aulosira and Tolypothrix are common in rice-field inocula. Composite starter cultures mix several species.

manas.q: Name two cyanobacteria genera used in rice.

children.note: Standing water, sunlight and neutral to slightly alkaline soil favour them. They are mainly a lowland rice technology.
They add organic matter, bind soil particles and release growth substances. They have also been used in salt-affected rice soils.
TNAU advises about 10 kg/ha of dried flakes mixed with 10 kg soil or sand, broadcast 7–10 days after transplanting.
Hold 3–4 inches of water for about a month after application so the algae can multiply.
TNAU reports about 20–30 kg N/ha under ideal conditions.

children.topic: Make your own: tray or field
children.note: Fill a shallow tray or small bunded plot with rice soil and water, add starter culture and a little superphosphate. After about two weeks, dry and collect the flakes.
Azolla is a tiny floating water fern that houses the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae in its leaves. Together they fix nitrogen and serve as green manure for rice.
Anabaena azollae lives in cavities of Azolla leaves and passes fixed nitrogen to the fern. It is passed on from one generation of the fern to the next.

manas.q: Which cyanobacterium lives inside Azolla leaves?

children.note: Azolla pinnata is widespread in Asia; Azolla filiculoides and others are also used.
Under good conditions it can double its mass in a few days, covering the water surface as a green mat.
Grow and incorporate fresh Azolla before transplanting; TNAU cites about 15 t/ha of fresh biomass.
Broadcast about 500 kg/ha fresh Azolla 7 days after transplanting and trample it in as it grows.

manas.q: When is Azolla added as a dual crop in rice (TNAU)?

children.note: TNAU reports about 40–60 kg N/ha per rice crop.
A small bunded plot with 10 cm water, cow dung slurry and a little superphosphate grows a harvest in 2–3 weeks.
The thick mat shades out some weeds. Azolla is also fed to cattle, poultry and fish.
Heat, strong sun, drying out, low phosphorus and insect pests slow it. It suits fields with assured water.
A filamentous actinomycete bacterium that forms N-fixing root nodules on certain non-legume trees and shrubs.
Plants nodulated by Frankia are called actinorhizal. Casuarina and alder (Alnus) are the best-known hosts.

manas.q: Which bacterium nodulates Casuarina?

children.note: Mainly relevant to agroforestry, windbreaks and land reclamation, not field crops.
Generic product types for these organisms; no brand matters as much as quality and freshness.
Bacteria mixed into a fine carrier such as lignite or peat. Cheap and easy to mix with seed, but shelf life is shorter.
Concentrated bacteria in liquid with protective additives. TNAU gives a shelf life of about 12–24 months.
TNAU wants carrier packets above 10⁹ cells/g at production and at least 10⁷ cells/g before expiry. Check the count and expiry date.

manas.q: Minimum cells/g in a carrier packet before expiry (TNAU)?

children.note: Mixtures of N-fixers, phosphate solubilizers and potash mobilizers in one pack. Convenient, but check each organism's count.
BGA is sold or made as dry soil-based flakes; Azolla is used fresh from a nursery.
Keep cool, dry and out of direct sun. Heat kills the bacteria faster than anything else.
Methods for Azospirillum and Gluconacetobacter; BGA and Azolla methods are in their own branches.
Mix the product with cooled rice gruel or jaggery solution, coat seeds evenly and dry in shade before sowing. TNAU suggests 200 ml liquid per acre of seed.
Dip seedling roots in a suspension (TNAU: two packets in 40 L water) for 5–10 minutes before transplanting.
Mix with well-rotted farmyard manure or compost, keep moist in shade overnight, then apply in furrows or at last ploughing.
Soak setts in a suspension of Gluconacetobacter or Azospirillum before planting, following the label.
Liquid products can go through drip lines; flush the system first and avoid mixing with chlorine or chemicals.
Do not mix with chemical fungicides, bactericides or strong fertilizers. If seed must be fungicide-treated, use a compatible one and apply bacteria last, or use soil application.

manas.q: Should Azospirillum be mixed with chemical fungicide?

children.note: Only conservative, well-established outcomes are listed here.
TNAU reports that Azospirillum can save about 25–30% of N fertilizer. Treat this as an upper guide, not a promise.

manas.q: How much N fertilizer can Azospirillum save (TNAU)?

children.note: Better roots and early vigour are the most consistent effects; yield gains in trials are usually modest.
Soil type, organic matter, moisture, strain quality and handling all change the response. Poor products give no effect.
Common errors and regulatory notes for India and Kenya.
No biofertilizer can feed a high-yield cereal crop alone. Use it to reduce, not eliminate, other N sources.
High doses of mineral N suppress biological nitrogen fixation, so bacteria add little.

manas.q: What happens to N fixation under heavy N fertilizer?

children.note: Leaving treated seed or packs in the sun, or using expired stock, kills the bacteria.
Biofertilizers such as Azospirillum, Acetobacter and BGA are covered by the Fertiliser (Control) Order, which sets minimum quality standards.
Buy only products registered with Kenya's regulators (e.g. KEPHIS for microbial products; biopesticides via PCPB). Ask the seller for the registration number.

nodeData.note: Soil bacteria and fungi that release phosphorus locked up as calcium, iron or aluminium phosphates. Used with compost and rock phosphate, they help crops get more from the phosphorus already in the soil.

children.topic: Why P gets locked in soil
children.note: Most soils hold plenty of total phosphorus, but only a tiny fraction is dissolved and available to roots at any time. Applied phosphate fertilizer is also quickly tied up.
Soil may contain hundreds of kg of P per hectare, yet roots can only take up phosphate dissolved in soil water, which is a very small share.

manas.q: Why can a soil rich in total P still be P-deficient?

children.note: In calcareous and alkaline soils, phosphate binds with calcium to form poorly soluble calcium phosphates.

manas.q: Which element locks P in alkaline soils?

children.note: In acid soils, common in Kenyan highlands and parts of India, phosphate binds tightly to iron and aluminium.

manas.q: Which elements lock P in acid soils?

children.note: A large part of soil P is in organic matter (e.g. phytate) and must be broken down by enzymes before plants can use it.
Phosphorus is most available around slightly acid to neutral pH (about 6–7). Liming acid soils and adding organic matter help.
Much of the phosphate from DAP or SSP is converted to insoluble forms within weeks, so crops use only part of it in the year applied.
Soil bacteria that release locked phosphate into forms roots can absorb. In India they are often sold as phosphobacteria.
A spore-forming bacterium; the variety phosphaticum is a classic PSB inoculant. Spores give it good survival in products.

manas.q: Which Bacillus species is the classic PSB inoculant?

children.note: A non-spore-forming PSB widely used in Indian inoculants.

manas.q: Name a Pseudomonas species used as PSB.

children.note: Bacillus subtilis, Bacillus circulans and other Pseudomonas strains also solubilise phosphate.
PSB are free-living, not symbiotic. They live in the rhizosphere where root exudates feed them.
Some soil fungi dissolve phosphate even more strongly than bacteria because they produce large amounts of organic acid.
A common black mould that produces citric and other acids; well studied for dissolving rock phosphate.

manas.q: Which Aspergillus species is a well-known phosphate solubilizer?

children.note: Listed by TNAU among phosphate-solubilizing fungi.
Penicillium strains (e.g. P. bilaiae in some countries) are used as phosphate-solubilizing inoculants.
Mycorrhizal fungi mainly extend roots to reach more phosphate; PSF dissolve it. Both can be used together.
Microbes use acids, enzymes and chelation to free phosphate.
They release gluconic, citric, oxalic and other acids that dissolve calcium phosphates and lower pH around the root.

manas.q: Name two organic acids PSB produce.

children.note: Organic acid anions grab iron, aluminium or calcium ions, freeing the phosphate that was bound to them.

manas.q: How do organic acids free P from iron and aluminium?

children.note: Enzymes such as phosphatases and phytase cut phosphate off organic compounds, mineralising organic P.

manas.q: Which enzymes release P from organic matter?

children.note: Many PSB also produce plant hormones and improve root growth, which adds to their benefit.
Rock phosphate is a cheap, natural, slow-release P source allowed in organic farming. PSB and organic matter help make it available.
It is mostly insoluble calcium phosphate, so it releases P slowly, especially in neutral or alkaline soils.

manas.q: Why is rock phosphate slow to release P?

children.note: Natural soil acidity dissolves rock phosphate more readily; in alkaline soils it needs microbial and organic help.
Mixing rock phosphate into compost heaps with PSB lets acids from decomposition dissolve it. The result is often called phosphorus-enriched compost.
TNAU suggests mixing 200 ml PSB with 400–600 kg cow dung/FYM and half a bag of rock phosphate, keeping it in shade overnight.

children.topic: Field signs: does the crop need P?
children.note: Recognise phosphorus shortage before reaching for any input; confirm with a soil test.
Older leaves turn dark green with purple or reddish tints, especially in maize and young seedlings in cold weather.

manas.q: What leaf colour signals P deficiency in maize?

children.note: Plants stay small with weak root systems and slow early growth.
P shortage delays flowering, seed set and maturity, and reduces grain filling.
Legumes short of P form fewer, smaller nodules and fix less nitrogen.

manas.q: How does P shortage affect legume nodulation?

children.note: Leaf colour can also come from cold, root damage or other nutrients. A soil test (Olsen or Bray P) confirms P status.
Better early vigour and rooting compared with an untreated strip. Effects are gradual and most visible where soil P is locked.
PSB suit almost all crops because every crop needs phosphorus.
Cereals, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, sugarcane and fruit trees can be treated. TNAU recommends PSB for all crops.
Phosphorus drives nodulation, so PSB plus Rhizobium is a common pulse package.
Many Kenyan highland soils fix P strongly to Fe and Al. Combine PSB with lime, manure and P fertilizer or rock phosphate.
Where soluble P fertilizers are not allowed, PSB with rock phosphate and compost is a main P strategy.
Generic product types; quality and freshness decide results.
PSB in a carrier such as lignite. Low cost and easy for seed coating.
Longer shelf life; TNAU gives about 12–24 months for liquid biofertilizers.
TNAU looks for above 10⁹ cells/g at production and at least 10⁷ cells/g before expiry for carrier products.
PSB combined with N-fixers and potash mobilizers in one product.
PSB carried on granules or added to compost and organic manures for soil application.
Keep in a cool, shaded, dry place; never in sun or near chemicals. Respect the expiry date.
PSB are applied the same ways as other bacterial biofertilizers.
Coat seed using a sticker such as rice gruel or jaggery, dry in shade and sow soon. TNAU: 200 ml liquid per acre of seed.
When seeds get both an N-fixer and PSB, coat with Rhizobium/Azospirillum first and PSB as the outer layer.

manas.q: Which goes on the seed last: Rhizobium or PSB?

children.note: Dip roots in a PSB suspension before transplanting; TNAU advises at least half an hour.
Mix with well-rotted manure or compost (with rock phosphate if available), keep moist overnight in shade, then apply in rows or at land levelling.
Liquid PSB can be applied by drip after flushing lines; avoid tank mixes with chemicals.
Keep away from chemical fungicides, bactericides and direct contact with concentrated fertilizers. Moist soil with organic matter helps them survive.
Conservative expectations only.

children.topic: Better use of soil and fertilizer P
children.note: PSB can increase the share of soil and applied P that crops take up. They do not create phosphorus, so very P-poor soils still need P inputs.

manas.q: Can PSB create phosphorus in a soil with none?

children.note: Trials commonly report modest yield gains; responses vary with soil pH, organic matter and product quality.
Responses are most reliable where PSB are applied with compost or manure, which feeds them.
Avoid these common problems.
PSB help unlock P but cannot replace all P inputs in low-P soils. Plan P from all sources.
Putting PSB under the N-fixer layer, or mixing with fungicide, reduces survival.
Applying to hot, dry soil without organic matter kills much of the inoculum.
In India PSB are covered by the Fertiliser (Control) Order; in Kenya buy only products registered with the national regulator (e.g. KEPHIS).

nodeData.note: Soil bacteria that unlock potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron already present in soil or minerals. They complement fertilisers and work best with organic matter and moisture.

children.note: A group of soil bacteria that do not add new nutrients but help release potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron that are already in the soil or in applied minerals.
Unlike nitrogen fixers, these microbes cannot create nutrients from air. They unlock nutrients locked in minerals, insoluble salts or organic matter so roots can absorb them.

manas.q: Do K, Zn and S microbes create new nutrients?

children.note: The common products contain free-living rhizosphere bacteria that live around roots and in soil, not inside plant nodules.
Many soils hold large total amounts of potassium and zinc, but only a small part is in a form roots can take up at any moment. Microbes help shift some of the locked pool into the available pool.
Potassium solubilising or mobilising bacteria release potassium from soil minerals such as micas and feldspars.
A Gram-negative bacterium widely sold in India as a potash mobilising biofertilizer, used in crops such as tea and sugarcane.

manas.q: Name a Gram-negative bacterium sold in India as a potash mobiliser.

children.note: Formerly called Bacillus mucilaginosus, this spore-forming bacterium coats itself in slime and weathers silicate minerals to release potassium. TNAU lists a potash strain of it.

manas.q: What is the newer name of Bacillus mucilaginosus?

children.note: Strains of Bacillus edaphicus, other Bacillus species, Pseudomonas and some fungi such as Aspergillus can also release potassium in lab and pot studies.
They release organic acids (such as citric, oxalic and gluconic acid) and slimy polysaccharides that dissolve and chelate the mineral surface, freeing potassium ions.

manas.q: What main chemical tool do KSB use to free potassium?

children.note: Most soil potassium sits inside mineral crystals. A smaller share is held on clay surfaces and only a tiny share is dissolved in soil water where roots can take it.
ZSB turn insoluble zinc compounds in soil, such as zinc oxide, carbonate and phosphate, into forms plants can absorb.
Mostly Bacillus and Pseudomonas strains, with some Gluconacetobacter and other rhizosphere bacteria. TNAU lists Bacillus as a silicate and zinc solubiliser.
They lower pH near roots by releasing acids (gluconic acid is common) and protons, and they make chelating compounds that keep zinc dissolved.

manas.q: Which organic acid is commonly linked with zinc solubilisation?

children.note: Zinc deficiency is common in alkaline, calcareous, sandy or eroded soils, in soils with very high phosphate, and in flooded rice fields.
ZSB work best when some zinc is present, for example native soil zinc or low-cost zinc oxide or zinc carbonate added to soil.
These bacteria convert elemental sulphur and other reduced sulphur forms into sulphate, the form plants take up.
Classic sulphur oxidisers. Thiobacillus thiooxidans is now named Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans; other Thiobacillus and many heterotrophic bacteria also oxidise sulphur.

manas.q: What is the current genus name for Thiobacillus thiooxidans?

children.note: They gain energy by oxidising sulphur to sulphuric acid. This supplies sulphate and slightly acidifies the zone around the sulphur particle.
They need a sulphur source to act on. They are typically paired with elemental sulphur, sulphur-coated products or gypsum-poor soils that receive sulphur.
The acid they produce can locally lower pH, which may improve availability of phosphorus and micronutrients in alkaline or sodic soils when enough sulphur is added.
Bacteria, mostly Bacillus species, that release silicon and other nutrients from silicate minerals.
Silicon is not essential for most crops but is beneficial, especially for rice and sugarcane. It strengthens cell walls, helps leaves stand upright and can reduce lodging and some pest attack.

manas.q: Which two crops benefit most from silicon?

children.note: Like KSB, they use organic acids and slimes to weather silicate minerals. One organism often releases both potassium and silicon.
Some bacteria help plants get iron and also starve pathogens of it by producing siderophores.
A small molecule that microbes release to grab ferric iron (Fe3+) very tightly. The iron-siderophore complex is then taken up by the microbe and sometimes by plants.

manas.q: What is a siderophore?

children.note: Pseudomonas fluorescens and related species make strong siderophores (pyoverdines). This is one reason they also act as biocontrol agents.
By locking up iron, siderophore producers can deprive root pathogens such as Fusarium and Pythium of iron, slowing their growth.

manas.q: How can siderophores help suppress root disease?

children.note: Knowing which leaves show symptoms first helps you tell nutrient problems apart. Confirm with a soil or leaf test before acting.
Yellowing then browning and scorching along the edges and tips of older, lower leaves, because K moves to new growth. Weak stems, lodging and poor fruit or grain fill follow.

manas.q: Where does potassium deficiency show first, and how?

children.note: Shows on young leaves: pale stripes or patches between veins, small narrow leaves, short internodes and a bunched rosette look. In maize it appears as white or pale bands near the leaf base.

manas.q: What are typical zinc deficiency signs?

children.note: A zinc deficiency disorder of rice in India: rusty brown spots on older leaves a few weeks after transplanting, with stunted, patchy growth.

manas.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes khaira disease in rice?

children.note: Even pale yellowing of the whole plant, often starting on younger leaves, because S moves less within the plant. It is easily confused with nitrogen deficiency, which starts on older leaves.

manas.q: How do you tell S deficiency from N deficiency?

children.note: Bright yellow tissue between green veins on the youngest leaves, common in calcareous or waterlogged soils.
Bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, sugarcane and tea take up large amounts of K. Oilseeds, onion, garlic and brassicas need extra S. Rice, maize and citrus are sensitive to Zn shortage.
Gradual effects: fewer deficiency symptoms over seasons, better leaf colour and steady soil and leaf test results. They will not cure an acute deficiency within days.
Mixed products combine nitrogen fixers, phosphate solubilisers and potash mobilisers in one pack.
Typically Azotobacter or Azospirillum for N, a phosphate solubiliser such as Bacillus megaterium for P, and Frateuria aurantia or a Paenibacillus for K. Some add ZSB.

manas.q: Which three groups of microbes make up an NPK consortium?

children.note: One application covers several functions and the strains can support each other. The strains must be tested to make sure they do not inhibit one another.
TNAU advises liquid potash mobilisers at about 200 ml per acre applied together with nitrogen fixers and phosphate solubilisers.
Sold as carrier powders, liquids and granules. Choose by how you will apply them and how long you need to store them. No brand names here.
Bacteria grown and mixed into a fine carrier such as lignite, talc or peat. Cheap and good for seed treatment and mixing with compost, but shorter shelf life.
Concentrated cells in a protective liquid. Usually keeps longer than powder and suits drip and seedling dips.
Microbes loaded onto granules for broadcasting or placing with seed, easy to handle with planters.
Look for the organism name, viable count (CFU per gram or ml), manufacture and expiry dates, batch number and registration number. In India, FCO sets minimum counts for KSB/KMB and ZSB.

manas.q: What five things should a biofertilizer label show?

children.note: Keep in a cool, shaded, dry place, away from direct sun, heat and chemicals. Use before the expiry date and do not store opened packs for long.
The same methods used for other bacterial biofertilizers apply here. Always follow the product label for the exact dose.
Make a slurry with a little cooled rice gruel or jaggery water as sticker, coat seed evenly, dry in shade and sow the same day.
Dip roots of transplanted seedlings such as rice, vegetables or onion in a dilute suspension for a short time before planting.
Mix the product with well-decomposed farmyard manure or compost, keep moist in shade for a few days, then apply in furrows or around plants.

manas.q: Why mix soil-applied biofertilizer with compost or FYM?

children.note: Liquid products can be injected through drip lines. Flush lines with clean water and avoid running them with chlorine or acid treatments.
TNAU suggests about 3 kg per acre of Frateuria aurantia as part of a tea biofertilizer package with Azospirillum, a P solubiliser and VAM.
Do not mix with chemical fungicides, bactericides or strong fertiliser solutions in the same tank or slurry. Keep a gap of several days between them.

manas.q: What should not be mixed with bacterial biofertilizers?

children.note: Microbes need moist soil and food. Apply into moist soil, ideally with organic matter, not onto dry, hot surface soil.
Gains are usually modest and build over time. These microbes complement, not fully replace, mineral fertiliser.
A TNAU tea package estimated that biofertilizers could save about 60 kg of muriate of potash per acre out of 200 kg recommended. Treat such figures as crop- and site-specific.
Benefits are more likely where available nutrients are low but total mineral reserves are present, and where organic matter supports microbial life.
Field results differ with soil type, pH, moisture, strain quality and crop. Run a simple side-by-side strip trial on your own farm.
Common misunderstandings that lead to disappointment with these products.
In sandy or highly weathered soils low in K minerals, there is little to mobilise. Such soils still need potassium inputs.

manas.q: Can KSB replace potash fertiliser on a sandy, K-poor soil?

children.note: Heat and age kill the cells. A product with a low live count will not perform.
Tank-mixing with fungicides, copper products or concentrated fertiliser can kill the bacteria before they reach the soil.
These microbes act slowly through the season. For a severe deficiency, correct it with a fertiliser or foliar spray first.
Rules and local context to keep in mind when making, selling or using these products.
The Fertiliser (Control) Order lists potash mobilising and zinc solubilising biofertilizers with quality standards. Products must meet these to be sold.
Check that a product is registered with the relevant Kenyan regulators. Products with pest or disease claims fall under the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB); KEPHIS oversees plant health.
Both countries have soil testing services. A soil test showing low available K, Zn or S tells you whether these microbes and matching nutrient inputs are worth trying.

nodeData.note: Soil fungi that partner with plant roots, extending them with fine hyphae to bring in phosphorus, zinc and water in exchange for plant sugars. Most crops benefit; protecting native fungi matters as much as adding inoculum.

children.note: Mycorrhiza means 'fungus-root': a partnership in which a soil fungus lives with plant roots and trades nutrients and water for plant sugars.
The plant feeds the fungus with sugars and fats made by photosynthesis. In return the fungus delivers phosphorus, other nutrients and water from soil the roots cannot reach.

manas.q: What does each partner give in a mycorrhizal symbiosis?

children.note: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) is found in most crops. Ectomycorrhiza is found mainly in forest trees such as pines and eucalyptus.
Fossils show this relationship dates back to the first land plants, which is why so many plant families carry it.
AMF grow inside root cortex cells and form tree-like structures called arbuscules. Older texts call them VAM (vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza).
Key genera are Rhizophagus (R. irregularis, formerly Glomus intraradices), Funneliformis (formerly Glomus mosseae), Glomus, Gigaspora and Acaulospora. Glomus is the most common.

manas.q: What is the current name of Glomus intraradices?

children.note: AMF belong to their own fungal group, the Glomeromycota. They do not form mushrooms.
Finely branched structures inside root cells where nutrients and sugars are exchanged.

manas.q: What are arbuscules?

children.note: Swollen, fat-filled sacs inside roots that act as food stores for the fungus.
Large, thick-walled resting spores formed in soil or roots. They survive dry seasons and start new colonies.
AMF cannot complete their life without a living host root, so they cannot be grown on lab media like bacteria. This makes inoculum harder to produce.

manas.q: Why is AMF inoculum harder to produce than bacterial biofertilizers?

children.note: In ectomycorrhiza the fungus wraps the root tip in a sheath and grows between, not into, root cells.
The fungal sheath around short roots is the mantle. The web of hyphae between outer root cells is the Hartig net, where exchange takes place.

manas.q: What are the two key structures of ectomycorrhiza?

children.note: Mainly pines, eucalyptus, oaks, birch and other forest trees. Many common forest mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of these fungi.
Pisolithus, Laccaria, Suillus, Rhizopogon and many others. Some are used in forestry nurseries.
Pines planted in new regions often grow poorly until their ectomycorrhizal partners are introduced, so nurseries inoculate seedlings.

children.topic: AM vs ecto at a glance
children.note: AM: inside cells, most crops, no mushrooms. Ecto: outside cells with a sheath, mostly trees, often produces mushrooms.

manas.q: How do AM and ectomycorrhiza differ?

children.note: The fungus acts like a giant extension of the root system.
Fungal threads are much finer than roots and grow several centimetres beyond them, exploring far more soil volume per gram of plant carbon.
Phosphate moves very slowly in soil, so roots quickly empty the soil next to them. Hyphae reach past this depleted zone and bring P back.

manas.q: Why are mycorrhizae especially good at improving P uptake?

children.note: AMF also improve uptake of other slow-moving nutrients, notably zinc and copper, and help with sulphur and nitrogen.
Hyphae enter fine soil pores roots cannot reach and keep supplying water as soil dries.
Hyphae can link neighbouring plants underground. How much they share resources is still being studied.
AMF help build stable soil crumbs.
A sticky glycoprotein linked to AMF hyphae, measured as glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP). It persists in soil for years.

manas.q: What is glomalin?

children.note: Hyphae physically bind soil particles and glomalin helps glue them, giving crumbly soil that resists erosion and lets water in.
Glomalin and hyphae add to stable soil organic carbon, which is one reason AMF matter in regenerative farming.
Benefits beyond nutrition, which vary with crop and conditions.
Mycorrhizal plants often cope better with dry spells because hyphae keep supplying water and nutrients from a larger soil volume.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizae help plants cope with drought?

children.note: Colonised roots can show less damage from some root rots and nematodes, partly through competition and stronger plant defences. Protection is partial, not a fungicide substitute.
Pre-colonised seedlings usually establish faster after transplanting.
Most crops form AM. A few families do not.
Maize, sorghum, millets, beans, cowpea, soybean, onion, leek, cassava, sweet potato, tomato, pepper, citrus, coffee, tea, banana and most fruit trees.
Crops with coarse roots and few root hairs, like onion, leek, citrus, cassava and many tree crops, depend most on mycorrhiza.

manas.q: Which kinds of crops depend most on mycorrhiza?

children.note: The cabbage family (cabbage, kale, mustard, canola) and the beet family (beet, spinach, amaranths) generally do not form AM. Lupins are also poor hosts.

manas.q: Which crop families do not form arbuscular mycorrhiza?

children.note: Low-P soils, eroded or newly levelled land, sterilised or soilless nursery media, and fields after long fallow or after non-host crops.
Stunted plants with dark green or purplish older leaves (phosphorus shortage) despite adequate P in the soil test may signal poor root uptake.
Colonisation cannot be seen by eye. Labs stain cleared roots and count infected root length under a microscope.
Because AMF need a host, inoculum is grown on host plant roots. No brand names here.
A mix of spores, colonised root pieces and hyphae in a carrier such as vermiculite, sand or clay granules.
Labels state viable propagules or spores per gram. Propagules include spores, hyphae and root bits that can start colonisation. Compare products by this count.

manas.q: What does 'propagules per gram' measure on a mycorrhiza label?

children.note: Finer spore powders suit seed coating and drip; granules suit furrow placement.
TNAU grows inoculum in polythene-lined trenches of vermiculite and soil with maize as the host, harvesting after about 60 days.
Keep cool and dry, out of sun. Spores are tougher than bacteria, but heat and moisture still reduce viability.
The fungus must touch roots. Place it in the root zone, not on the surface.
TNAU suggests about 100 g of bulk inoculum per square metre mixed into the nursery bed before sowing.
Mix about 5–10 g of inoculum into each bag of potting mix, per TNAU guidance.
Place about 20 g per seedling in the planting hole, under and around the roots, per TNAU guidance.

manas.q: Where should mycorrhizal inoculum be placed at transplanting?

children.note: TNAU gives about 200 g per tree, placed into holes or trenches dug in the active root zone.
Place in the seed furrow or coat seed so spores sit beside young roots. Tea guidance from TNAU is about 4 kg per acre.
Works well with compost, Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Rhizobium and PSB. Keep chemical fungicides away from the root zone at application.
Many common practices reduce native and introduced mycorrhiza.
When soluble P is plentiful the plant stops feeding the fungus and colonisation drops. Use moderate P, ideally banded.

manas.q: Why does heavy P fertiliser reduce mycorrhiza?

children.note: Several soil-applied and systemic fungicides harm AMF. Avoid drenches and in-furrow fungicides where inoculum is used.
Ploughing tears the hyphal network and dilutes spores, so plants must rebuild colonisation each season.

manas.q: How does tillage harm mycorrhiza?

children.note: Without living roots AMF starve. After long fallow, crops can show P deficiency even in fertile soil ('long fallow disorder').

manas.q: What is long fallow disorder?

children.note: A season of brassicas or beet lowers spore numbers for the next crop.
Waterlogged paddies and soil fumigation or solarisation sharply reduce AMF.
Often the cheapest route is to protect the fungi already in your soil.
Grow cover crops or intercrops between main crops so AMF always have a host.
Minimum or zero tillage keeps networks intact.
Follow non-host crops with strong hosts like maize, sorghum or legumes to rebuild spores.
Results are real but vary widely. Mycorrhiza is not a fertiliser and adds no P of its own.
Responses are largest in P-poor soils, in sterilised nursery media and in highly dependent crops, and smallest in high-P soils.
In fields with healthy native AMF, added inoculum may give little extra benefit. Test with untreated strips on your own farm.
Mycorrhiza can let you use P more efficiently and sometimes reduce P rates, but crops still need adequate nutrients overall.
Common errors with mycorrhizal products.
Spores scattered on dry surface soil rarely reach roots. Always place inoculum in the root zone.
Inoculating cabbage, kale or beet wastes money because they are non-hosts.
Heavy soluble P at the same time cancels much of the benefit.
Once roots are colonised, extra inoculum adds little. Placement and quality matter more than quantity.
Local context for using mycorrhiza.
Mycorrhizal biofertilizers are covered by the Fertiliser (Control) Order, which sets quality standards that products must meet.
Check that products are registered with the relevant Kenyan regulators (KEPHIS; PCPB where pest or disease claims are made).
Fruit tree, tea, coffee and forestry nurseries in both countries are the most practical starting point for inoculation.
Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

nodeData.note: Biofertilizers and biopesticides are living products. They only work if they arrive alive, are applied the right way, and are used as part of a wider soil and crop plan.

children.topic: What they are – and are not
children.note: Clear definitions help set honest expectations with farmers.
A product containing live, beneficial microbes that improve nutrient supply to the crop, by fixing nitrogen or releasing locked-up P, K or Zn.

manas.q: What is a biofertilizer?

children.note: A product based on living microbes (fungi, bacteria, viruses) or natural substances that control pests or diseases, e.g. Trichoderma, Bacillus, Beauveria, Bt.

manas.q: Give three examples of microbial biopesticides.

children.note: Seaweed extracts, humic substances and some microbes that improve plant growth or stress tolerance, without being a nutrient source or pesticide.
A biofertilizer bag contains few nutrients itself. It works through microbes over weeks, not overnight like urea.

manas.q: Why does a biofertilizer not act as fast as urea?

children.note: Compost and manure are organic fertilisers that feed soil. Biofertilizers are specific, counted microbes; compost is often their best partner.
They complement good nutrition and crop protection. On very poor soils or severe outbreaks they help but rarely solve the problem alone.
The common organisms sold as bio-inputs, by job.
Rhizobium (legumes), Azotobacter and Azospirillum (cereals, vegetables), Gluconacetobacter (sugarcane), blue-green algae and Azolla (rice).
PSB such as Bacillus and Pseudomonas dissolve soil P; AM fungi carry P to roots through their hyphae.
KMB release potassium, ZSB release zinc, and sulfur-oxidising bacteria convert elemental S into sulfate.
Trichoderma (fungus) and Pseudomonas fluorescens, Bacillus subtilis (bacteria) protect roots and seeds from soil-borne diseases.
Beauveria, Metarhizium and Lecanicillium fungi, Bt bacteria and insect viruses such as NPV infect specific pests.
Purpureocillium (Paecilomyces) lilacinum and some Pochonia and Bacillus strains attack nematode eggs or juveniles.
The carrier keeps microbes alive from factory to field and makes them easy to apply.
Traditional powders for bacterial biofertilizers. Naturally acidic, so neutralised with lime, ground fine and sterilised before inoculation.
Common carrier for Trichoderma and Pseudomonas powders used in seed and soil treatment.
Broth with protective additives. Easy to use in drip and seed treatment and usually longer shelf life than powders.

manas.q: Name two advantages of liquid biofertilizers.

children.note: Microbes on granular carriers for broadcasting with seed or fertiliser drills; convenient for large fields.
Used for AM fungi, which must be grown on living roots and are sold as spores and root bits in a mineral carrier.
Cheap, locally available, rich in organic matter, high water-holding, free of toxic substances and easy to sterilise.
Quality is about live, correct organisms in enough numbers, without contaminants.
Colony-forming units: the number of live microbial cells per gram or millilitre that can grow on a lab plate. It measures life, not weight.

manas.q: What does CFU stand for and what does it measure?

children.note: India's Fertiliser (Control) Order lists biofertilizers with minimum viable counts, pH, moisture, particle size and contamination rules. Check the current schedule as it is amended over time.
Classic FCO norms require about 5×10⁷ CFU per gram for carrier products and 1×10⁸ CFU per ml for liquids; some organisms have their own values.

manas.q: What minimum counts does the FCO set for carrier and liquid biofertilizers?

children.topic: Count at expiry, not just at making
children.note: TNAU guidance aims for over 10⁹ cells/g at preparation and at least 10⁷ cells/g before expiry, because counts fall during storage.
Good products should show no contaminating organisms at high dilution; TNAU cites none at the 10⁻⁶ level. Contaminants compete and may be harmful.

manas.q: Why do contamination limits matter in biofertilizers?

children.note: Check organism name, CFU count, batch number, manufacture and expiry dates, crop, dose and registration number. Missing details are a warning sign.
Government labs (in India, central and regional biofertilizer labs) sample products from the market; companies should keep their own batch tests.
Microbes die faster in heat and sunlight; storage decides what reaches the farmer alive.
Store in a cool, dry, shaded place away from direct sun, fertilisers and pesticides. Never leave in a hot vehicle or on a shop window.

manas.q: What are the key storage rules for biofertilizers?

children.note: Usually have shorter shelf life than liquids; counts drop steadily, so sell and use fresh stock first.
TNAU reports liquid biofertilizers holding counts for 12–24 months when kept away from heat and light.
Expired packs may contain few live cells; selling them damages trust in all bio-inputs.
Rotate stock in stores and agro-dealer shops by expiry date, not by arrival.
Thin polythene bags allow gas exchange for carrier products; do not puncture liquid bottles or leave them open.
The goal is to place live microbes where roots will grow, at the right time.
Make a slurry with a sticker such as cooled rice gruel or jaggery water, coat seed, dry in shade, and sow the same day.

manas.q: How is a biofertilizer applied as seed treatment?

children.note: Dip roots of transplanted crops (rice, vegetables) in a suspension of the biofertilizer for a short time before planting.
Mix the product with dried, powdered FYM or compost, keep moist overnight, and spread in furrows or at planting.
Liquid formulations can be injected through drip after flushing out chemicals; keep filters clean and avoid chlorinated water.
Dip sugarcane setts, potato seed tubers or cuttings in the suspension before planting so roots start among the microbes.
Add AM fungi or bacteria to nursery beds and potting mix, or to the root zone of existing trees.
Apply at or just before sowing or planting, in moist soil, in the cool part of the day. Biopesticides usually work best as prevention.
What can and cannot be mixed with living products.
Chemical fungicides can kill fungal products like Trichoderma, and copper and antibiotics can kill bacteria. Do not mix them in one tank or slurry.

manas.q: Why must Trichoderma not be mixed with chemical fungicides?

children.note: If seed must be dressed with a fungicide, treat with the chemical first and the biofertilizer later, as TNAU advises.
Concentrated chemical fertilisers can harm microbes on contact. Apply them separately in time or place, not in the same mix.
Different bacterial biofertilizers, such as Azospirillum and PSB, are commonly mixed and applied together.
Many bacteria and Trichoderma can be used together, but some strains inhibit each other. Follow tested combinations or the maker's chart.
Compost, FYM and vermicompost carry and feed microbes. Mixing bio-inputs with them is generally safe and helpful.

manas.q: Which inputs are generally the best partners for biofertilizers?

children.note: Compatibility differs by strain and product. Rely on the label or a tested compatibility chart, not on guesswork.
Products containing several organisms with different jobs.
A single product mixing, for example, an N-fixer, a P-solubiliser and a K-mobiliser, often sold as 'NPK bio' liquid.
One product does several jobs, saving labour, and partners can support each other in the root zone.
Strains must be tested for compatibility; each organism still needs to meet its own count. More organisms is not automatically better.
Combining organic, biological and mineral sources to feed crops and build soil.
Use compost or manure, biofertilizers, legumes and, where allowed, measured mineral fertiliser together, based on soil tests.

manas.q: What is integrated nutrient management?

children.note: They can supply or release part of the N, P or K need and improve efficiency; they rarely meet a high-yield crop's full need alone.
In certified organic farming, INM means compost, green manure, rotations, bio-inputs and approved minerals only.
Benefits grow as organic matter and microbial life rebuild; judge results over several seasons, not one.
Bio-inputs are regulated products. Selling unregistered products risks seizure and loss of trust.
The Pest Control Products Board registers pest control products, including microbial biopesticides, before they can be sold.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body registers biopesticides?

children.note: KEPHIS handles plant health and inspection, including import permits for live organisms and biocontrol agents and quality checks on inputs.
The Kenya Bureau of Standards sets and enforces product standards, including standards relevant to organic fertilisers and soil inputs.
Biofertilizers and organic fertilisers are covered by the Fertiliser (Control) Order, which sets specifications and requires registration and labelling.

manas.q: Which order regulates biofertilizer quality in India?

children.note: In India, biopesticides are registered under the Insecticides Act through the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC).
KOAN supports organic farming in Kenya; small farmer groups can use Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS) for local organic markets.
The East African Organic Products Standard (EAS 456) is the regional organic standard, linked to the Kilimohai organic mark.
NPOP sets standards for third-party organic certification and exports; PGS-India is a lower-cost, group-based system for domestic markets.
Organic farms must confirm that a bio-input is allowed (non-GMO, approved carrier and additives) with their certifier or PGS group.
Honest, practical advice builds repeat customers and protects the whole category.
Ask about the crop, soil, symptoms and past inputs, then recommend a product that fits, not the most expensive one.
Tell farmers it is alive: keep it cool and shaded, use before expiry, and do not mix with chemicals.

manas.q: What three handling messages should every farmer hear about bio-inputs?

children.note: Promise gradual soil and crop benefits, not instant green-up. Over-promising leads to disappointment.
Side-by-side plots on a farmer's own field are the most convincing proof; keep simple yield and cost records.
Demonstrate seed treatment or root dip in person; many failures come from wrong application.
Visit or call after planting to check results and correct mistakes; satisfied farmers become your best promoters.
Errors that make good products fail in the field.
Overdosing wastes money; correct placement and live counts matter more than quantity.
Heat on shop shelves or in vehicles kills microbes before sale.
Microbes need moisture to survive and multiply; applying to dry soil without organic matter often fails.
Some biopesticides affect non-target insects or need protective gear; follow the label.
Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.
